title: IBDV Reverse Genetics Rescue System and Neutralization Assay in Chicken B Cells
author: Reddy, Nazki, et al.
materials: pIBDV‐A and pIBDV‐B (Gene Art; Thermo Fisher Scientific)
Escherichia coli DH5α (New England Biolabs: NEB® 5‐alpha competent E. coli; C2984H, high efficiency)
LB agar plate supplemented with 5 μg/ml ampicillin
LB broth supplemented with 5 μg/ml ampicillin (Gibco, cat. no. 10855‐021)
Maxi plasmid purification kit (Qiagen, cat. no. 12162)
KpnI‐HF® restriction enzyme (New England Biolabs, cat. no. R3142S)
NheI‐HF® restriction enzyme (New England Biolabs, cat. no. R3131S)

Reverse genetics has been widely used to generate infectious molecular clones of viruses entirely from a full‐length cDNA copy of the viral genome. Reverse genetics systems for IBDV rely on the transfection of cells with two plasmids, one encoding IBDV segment A and one encoding segment B. In each plasmid, immediately upstream of the coding region and the 5′ noncoding region, is a self‐cleaving hammerhead ribozyme, and immediately downstream of the coding region and 3′ noncoding region is a self‐cleaving hepatitis delta ribozyme sequence. When cells are co‐transfected with both plasmids, VP1 is transcribed from segment B and translated, and VP2, VP3, VP4, and VP5 are transcribed from segment A and translated. In addition, the VP1 polymerase replicates the genome from the cleaved RNA sequence. Traditionally, immortalized cell lines, such as chicken embryo fibroblasts (CEFs) or DF‐1, QM7, or Vero cells, have been transfected with the plasmids to rescue cell‐culture‐adapted IBDV strains (Mendez et al., 2017; Mundt & Vakharia, 1996; Yao, Goodwin, & Vakharia, 1998; Zierenberg et al., 2004). In order to rescue a field strain of IBDV, researchers have in the past inoculated transfected CEFs or DF‐1 cell lysates into birds either intramuscularly (Nouen et al., 2012) or directly into the BF (Yu et al., 2012). Although these techniques successfully generated molecular clones of field strains 8818 and HLJ0504, respectively, they were laborious, required facilities for in vivo studies, and suffered from potential animal welfare issues. Recently, we and others demonstrated that field strains of IBDV can replicate within primary chicken bursal cells isolated from the BF and cultured in the presence of CD40L or phorbol 12‐myristate 13‐acetate (PMA) (Delgui, Gonzalez, & Rodriguez, 2009; Dulwich et al., 2017, 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Soubies et al., 2018; Terasaki et al., 2008). Furthermore, it was shown that the cell lysates from transfected DF‐1 cells could be passaged onto chicken primary bursal cells to rescue a molecular clone of a field strain (Cubas‐Gaona et al., 2020), which negated the need to inoculate chickens; but chickens were still needed to provide the primary bursal cells. The immortalized chicken B‐cell line DT40 has also been used to sustain IBDV field strains (Delgui, Gonzalez, et al., 2009; Terasaki et al., 2008), and here, we extend these observations by describing the rescue of a molecular clone of IBDV by electroporation of DT40 cells, bypassing the use of DF‐1 cells. Our laboratory recently used this protocol to rescue a panel of recombinant chimeric IBDVs containing the HVRs of diverse field strains in the backbone of the lab‐adapted strain PBG98 (Reddy et al., 2022).

steps.title: Design and synthesize plasmids
steps.instruction: Create reverse‑genetics plasmids containing a hammerhead ribozyme, the 5′ non‑coding region, the full‑length coding region of IBDV segment A or B, the 3′ non‑coding region, and a hepatitis‑delta ribozyme, all under a CMV promoter; typically use the pSF‑CAG‑KAN vector.

steps.title: Clone inserts into expression vector
steps.instruction: Obtain commercially synthesized inserts, digest with appropriate restriction enzymes, and ligate them into the multiple‑cloning site of pSF‑CAG‑KAN; then verify that the cloned insert sizes are 3.4 kb for segment A and 3.1 kb for segment B and confirm sequence by Sanger sequencing.

steps.title: Prepare healthy DT40 cells
steps.instruction: Thaw DT40 cells from liquid nitrogen, then split the culture at least two to three times to ensure healthy, actively dividing cells before any manipulation.

steps.title: Optimize electroporation settings
steps.instruction: Determine the optimal electroporation voltage (150–300 V) and pulse duration (1–5 ms) for DT40 cells to maximize plasmid uptake while minimizing cell death.

steps.title: Electroporate DT40 cells with plasmids
steps.instruction: Using the optimized settings, electroporate DT40 cells with the two reverse‑genetics plasmids pRG‑PBG98‑A and pRG‑PBG98‑B to rescue infectious IBDV.

steps.title: Calculate DT40 cell density for assay
steps.instruction: Determine the appropriate DT40 cell concentration to add to each virus‑serum mixture (exact density calculated based on well format and desired multiplicity of infection).

steps.title: Prepare virus‑serum mixtures
steps.instruction: Mix 100 TCID₅₀ of the rescued IBDV (or cell‑culture‑adapted virus) with heat‑inactivated serum that has been serially diluted; include positive and negative serum and virus controls in every experiment.

steps.title: Add DT40 cells and incubate
steps.instruction: Add the calculated number of healthy DT40 cells to each virus‑serum mixture, incubate the cultures for 4 days, then inspect for the presence or absence of cytopathic effect to determine the virus neutralization titer.
